findings.description: The bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so stored objects (including the seeded vendor roster) are not guaranteed to be encrypted with a managed or customer-managed KMS key.
No ACL is specified and no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is attached, leaving the bucket exposed to accidental public ACLs or bucket policies granting anonymous access.
The bucket has no logging block, so object-level access to archived reports leaves no audit trail, defeating detection of unauthorised reads.
Versioning is not enabled, so objects can be overwritten or deleted without recovery, and with force_destroy = true the entire bucket and its contents can be deleted by a terraform destroy.
The ledger export bucket defines no server_side_encryption_configuration, so sensitive financial export data is stored without enforced encryption at rest.
No logging block is configured for the ledger bucket, so access to financial exports is not recorded for audit or incident investigation.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource restricts public ACLs or policies on this bucket, so a later ACL or policy change could expose ledger data publicly.
Versioning is absent on a bucket holding ledger exports, so tampering or deletion of records cannot be detected or rolled back.
The model artifacts bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration, so artifacts that may be loaded into production inference are stored unencrypted by default.
The bucket lacks an associated aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, leaving no account-level guardrail against public ACLs or bucket policies.
Operational runbooks frequently contain sensitive procedural and connection details, yet this bucket defines no server-side encryption configuration.
No logging block is present, so reads and writes to runbook content are not auditable.
No public access block is configured, so the bucket is not protected against future public ACL or policy grants.

findings.issue_category: no public access block on log bucket
findings.description: The audit/log-delivery bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so the security log destination could be exposed publicly by an ACL or policy change; log data is highly sensitive.
The audit trail bucket sets force_destroy = true and has no object lock / MFA delete, so audit logs can be irrevocably destroyed by a terraform destroy, undermining the integrity of the audit record.
The object is uploaded with no kms_key_id or server_side_encryption argument into a bucket that lacks default encryption, so the vendor roster data is stored in plaintext.
